content: Patient monitoring tools should incorporate data on individuals who initiate treatment late or disengage from care. These tools should track demographic, clinical, laboratory, adherence, and psychosocial criteria to assess and document eligibility for differentiated service delivery (DSD). It is also essential to monitor which DSD elements are being provided, such as antiretroviral therapy (ART) refills, clinical monitoring, and adherence support, as well as the location of service delivery (e.g., community, clinic, pharmacy, or laboratory). Electronic medical records (EMRs) and patient monitoring tools should record key data points, including ART drug pick-up dates, the quantity of ART dispensed, and other services provided, such as psychosocial support, adherence counseling, or laboratory testing. These tools should also include data elements for HIV treatment and care cards or folders to facilitate DSD monitoring. However, many of these data points are not routinely captured in current medical records or EMR systems, necessitating updates to these systems in many settings. DSD models are continuously evolving, requiring patient monitoring tools and EMR systems to adapt flexibly. Facilities relying on paper records must revise ART registers or create new registers specific to DSD models to track uptake and outcomes. Since DSD-related data may change over time, it should be organized chronologically, such as monthly, from the initiation of DSD services. Key DSD elements for periodic recording in HIV patient monitoring include: Date of DSD eligibility assessment. Patient DSD eligibility classification (e.g., established on ART or not, eligible or ineligible for DSD, with reasons for ineligibility such as viral load >1000 copies/mL). DSD start date. DSD model (e.g., fast-track ART refills, facility adherence clubs, community ART groups, or virtual approaches like teleconsultations or automated dispensing machines). Group ID for individuals in group DSD models. ART pick-up dates and quantities dispensed. Types of other medications picked up alongside ART (e.g., TB preventive treatment) and their dates. HIV clinic visit dates. Viral load test results and dates. Additional information, such as adherence monitoring and symptom development. Whether the client is still receiving DSD services. Whether the client has switched between DSD models and the reasons for the switch. Reasons for exclusion from DSD models, such as pregnancy, opportunistic infections, increased viral load, healthcare worker concerns, adverse drug reactions, or patient preference. Exclusions may be temporary, with reassessments conducted per national guidelines. For community ART services, monitoring considerations include the development, use, and storage of facility and community tools. HIV patient cards or folders and paper or electronic registers should remain at the facility. Since community-based DSD models lack monitoring tools at the point of service delivery, new tools must be developed and implemented. These tools should be simple, user-friendly, and capable of tracking DSD ART services and client follow-up. Data confidentiality and security are critical in community settings. Paper-based systems should use numeric codes or other identifiers to avoid unintended disclosure of HIV status. Both paper and electronic reports must be securely stored or transmitted promptly to health facilities. For longitudinal data collection and submission, secure electronic tools, such as tablets or mobile applications, are recommended. Effective data flow between community-delivered services and health facilities is essential for patient management and care. Data from community ART tools should be abstracted and transmitted to health facilities in near real-time for transcription and entry into the HIV patient monitoring system. This includes updating HIV treatment and care cards or folders and EMRs where applicable. Introducing new tools and roles under DSD may increase the risk of errors, missing data, and delayed submissions. Conventional data quality improvement strategies should be adapted to these new tools and approaches. These strategies include identifying data elements to assess, sampling records, comparing values across paper and electronic systems, and re-counting aggregate tallies. Joint community and facility data quality assessments should be conducted, incorporating activities that evaluate both the quality of care and data for DSD services. Mozambique provides an example of strengthening HIV patient monitoring systems to support DSD implementation. The country standardized the registration of DSD services in its paper-based master card system, coding various DSD models for efficient tracking. For individuals enrolled in multiple models, priority is given to recording models with the most significant impact on ART service planning and management, such as multi-month drug dispensing and community drug dispensing. Mozambique also uses an EMR system in high-volume facilities, covering over 80% of people living with HIV on ART. Data from paper master cards are entered daily into the EMR, which includes standard DSD indicators such as the percentage of eligible clients enrolled in DSD and the percentage of clients enrolled in at least one DSD model. These indicators are disaggregated by location, age, and DSD model type and are reviewed monthly to improve service delivery. The country conducts annual DSD data performance reviews to complement routine monitoring. These reviews assess health facility and client coverage of DSD, service quality, retention, viral load suppression, and perceptions of DSD services. Data are collected from a representative sample of facilities and analyzed to inform action plans for improving performance. All patient monitoring systems must adhere to data protection and confidentiality frameworks. Individual-level information related to stigmatized or criminalized behaviors should not be included in ART registers or reported to higher data management units. Such information should only be recorded in clinical records if clinically relevant and must be kept secure and confidential. Clients should be assured of the security and confidentiality of their medical records.
